analysis.one_liner: Mandates federal oil and gas lease sales offshore and onshore, with weakened environmental review.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee on June 24, 2022 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ordered the Interior Department to hold specific Gulf of Mexico and Cook Inlet offshore lease sales by June 30, 2022, finalize a 2022-2027 offshore leasing program with at least 11 sales, and immediately resume onshore lease sales — with a minimum of four sales per year in Wyoming, New Mexico, Colorado, Utah, Montana, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Nevada, and any other eligible state. It would have exempted those lease sales from the National Environmental Policy Act, capped how long environmental reviews could take whenever average gasoline exceeded $3.99 a gallon, and stripped any project of environmental review altogether if the agency missed the deadline. If Interior missed the deadlines, the bill would have frozen its hiring and staffing.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies gain the most: the bill orders the government to put federal offshore and onshore leases up for auction on a fixed schedule, requires that every eligible parcel in a state be offered, and exempts those sales from environmental review. Supporters argued drivers would benefit from more domestic supply at a time of high gasoline prices in 2022.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires Interior to hold Lease Sale 258 in the Cook Inlet area and Lease Sales 259 and 261 in the Gulf of Mexico by June 30, 2022, and to finalize a 2022-2027 offshore leasing program with at least 11 sales.

Onshore, it orders the immediate resumption of lease sales and a minimum of four sales per year in Wyoming, New Mexico, Colorado, Utah, Montana, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Nevada, and other eligible states, offering all eligible parcels.
Lease sales and the new leasing program would not count as major federal actions under the National Environmental Policy Act, shielding them from the environmental review process.

Whenever the national average gas price exceeded $3.99, environmental assessments would have to be finished within one year and impact statements within two; if an agency missed the deadline, the project would no longer be subject to NEPA at all.
If Interior missed the leasing deadlines, the bill would bar new hires, new positions, and reassignments at the department until it complied.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the costs would fall on taxpayers and on communities near federal lands and coastal waters, which would lose the environmental review process for lease sales; the government would also lose discretion to weigh drilling against fishing, recreation, and conservation uses of public lands and waters. The bill includes no mechanism ensuring companies that win leases actually produce oil or lower prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near public lands and coasts

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts offshore lease sales and the leasing program from environmental review under NEPA, and would strip even the ordinary review from any project whose paperwork missed a deadline during high gas prices — meaning some projects could proceed with no federal environmental analysis at all.

Mandating lease sales does not guarantee drilling or lower prices: companies can win leases and leave them undeveloped, so the promised relief at the pump was speculative. Millions of acres of existing federal leases were already unused, a fact the bill does not address.

The hiring-freeze penalty would have punished Interior employees as a group by freezing staffing whenever the department missed deadlines, without addressing any underlying budget or staffing constraint.

The strongest good-faith objection in favor: with gasoline above $4 a gallon nationally in mid-2022, supporters argued that pausing federal leasing was needlessly constraining domestic supply, and that agencies' environmental reviews take years and delay projects regardless of merit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits — more lease auctions and the promise of more supply — were indirect and uncertain, since leasing does not require production. Its costs were concrete: removing environmental review from lease sales on public lands and coastal waters, and automatically ending review for projects that missed arbitrary deadlines. The design favored speed-to-auction over any balancing of drilling against other public uses.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Lauren Boebert introduced the bill on June 24, 2022, joined by seven Republican cosponsors, all in the House.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources — the only action it ever received.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote was ever scheduled, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, oil and gas companies received none of the mandated lease sales, blanket parcel offerings, or environmental-review exemptions. Communities and businesses that use or depend on federal lands and coastal waters — and the public more broadly — were spared the bill's changes, while drivers saw no benefit from it either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities near public lands and coastal waters

for.name: 7 of 213 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill: Reps. Rosendale, Tiffany, Gohmert, Gosar, Nehls, Biggs, and Perry.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Raúl Grijalva, D-AZ)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 24, 2022 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors were Republicans and no Democrat cosponsored the bill; it never reached a vote, so no roll call shows where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill would have ordered fixed-schedule auctions of federal offshore and onshore leases, required every eligible parcel to be offered, and exempted those sales from environmental review — expanding access to public resources at the public's environmental expense. There is no requirement that leased acreage be drilled or that production lower consumer prices.

industries.industry: Commercial fishing and coastal tourism businesses
industries.note: Mandated sales in the Gulf of Mexico and Cook Inlet, exempted from environmental review, would remove the process that weighs drilling against fishing grounds and coastal economies that share those waters.

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation and conservation interests on public lands
industries.note: Annual mandatory lease sales across nine western and plains states, with all eligible parcels offered, would put lands used for recreation and conservation up for drilling with no discretion to hold them back.
